h1: Becoming a beer buyer for a bar or restaurant group
title: Becoming a Beer Buyer for a Bar Group | Craft Beer School
desc: What a beer buyer for a bar or restaurant group does: building the list, choosing suppliers, freshness, pour cost, staff training and how to get in.
teaser: A beer buyer decides what a group's guests drink. It is part palate, part spreadsheet and part negotiation.
standfirst: Restaurant and bar groups with several outlets often have one person deciding which beers go on the list. The job mixes tasting, supplier relationships, margin maths and logistics. Here is what it involves and how people get there.
sections:
A beer buyer builds and manages the beer list across a group's outlets. That means choosing which beers to stock on draught and in packaged formats, negotiating with breweries and distributors, setting prices with the finance team and making sure the beer arrives fresh and is served well.

In smaller groups this sits with a bar manager or a beverage manager who also buys wine and spirits. Larger groups may have a dedicated beer or beverage buyer. Either way, the job connects the guest's glass to the supplier's invoice.

A good list has a reason for every line. Most groups need a reliable lager that most guests will order, a wheat beer, a pale ale or IPA for craft drinkers and something darker or unusual. The mix depends on the concept: a sports bar, a fine dining restaurant and a brewpub style gastropub need very different lists.

Food matters too. A North Indian grill menu with smoky tandoori dishes suits crisp lagers and malty ambers. A coastal seafood menu leans towards wheat beers and lighter ales. Our beer styles guide is a handy reference when you are matching styles to a menu.

Fewer lines often work better. Every tap needs a keg that turns over fast enough to stay fresh. A list of twenty taps in a quiet outlet means beer sitting in kegs for weeks.

Buyers think in pour cost: the cost of the beer in a serve divided by the price the guest pays. The working is simple. Divide the keg price by the number of saleable serves, then divide that by the menu price.

Saleable serves are the catch. A 50 litre keg holds about 151 servings of 330 ml in theory. In practice, line cleaning, foam on the first pours of a new keg, spillage and staff tasting take some of it. If only 135 serves reach guests, every serve costs more than the paper figure. A buyer who tracks yield by outlet finds the bar with a foaming system or a heavy handed pourer quickly.

Packaged beer is easier to count but takes fridge space and stocks age. Rotate it on packaging dates, as a good bottle shop would.

How beer reaches a bar varies by state. In some states licensed outlets buy through licensed distributors or wholesalers, while others route supply through a state agency. Brand registration, pricing rules and permitted pack sizes also differ. A buyer working across several states learns each system or works closely with someone who knows it. Rules change, so check the current position with your excise team or licensing consultant.

Freshness is the buyer's quiet responsibility. Ask suppliers for packaging dates on every delivery. Hop forward beers lose aroma within weeks if stored warm. Know how your distributor stores and transports beer, because a lorry that sits in the sun for a day undoes the brewery's work. Our guide to beer shelf life explains what goes wrong.

A buyer can choose perfect beers and still see them fail if staff cannot describe or serve them. Short tastings for servers, a one-line description per beer and basic serving standards make a big difference. Clean glasses, the right serving temperature and a proper head change how a beer tastes to the guest.

Draught quality is part of the buyer's job even when someone else cleans the lines. Agree a cleaning schedule with every outlet or service provider and check the records. A beer that tastes buttery or sour on tap often points to dirty lines rather than a bad batch. The brewery will rightly ask about it before accepting a complaint.

Tastings for staff should be small, educational and within company policy, with spit cups available and nobody pressed to drink.

Most beer buyers come up through hospitality: bartender, bar manager, beverage manager. Some come from brewery sales or distribution, bringing supplier knowledge. A few come from purchasing roles in hotels or retail.

The useful mix is a trained palate, comfort with spreadsheets and the confidence to negotiate. Sensory qualifications such as the BJCP judging programme or Cicerone certification help you describe beer with authority. Our guide to the BJCP exam covers one route.

Understanding how beer is brewed helps more than people expect. When a supplier says a batch is "a bit different", a buyer who knows what diacetyl or oxidation tastes like can judge whether it should be on the list at all.

Pick a bar you know and write out its beer list. Next to each beer, note the style, the format and who you think orders it. Then mark the lines you would cut. You have just done a buyer's first range review.
faqs: What does a beer buyer for a restaurant group do?
Chooses which beers the group stocks, negotiates with suppliers, sets prices with finance, checks freshness and trains staff to serve the list well.
The cost of the beer in a serve divided by the price the guest pays. Buyers track it by outlet to spot losses from foaming systems or poor pouring.
How do people become beer buyers?
Usually through bar work and bar or beverage management, sometimes from brewery sales or purchasing. A trained palate and good numeracy both matter.
